title: The Houses of Unequal Stars
summary: An intentional community mistakes a useful star classification for social destiny while a provisional boundary becomes an inherited border.

entries.title: Fen of the Rotating Tables
entries.body:
Fen proposed changing unpopular tasks every seventh day, then exempted skilled scribes from rotation. Workers challenged the exception without rejecting the community. Her revised notes admit that inclination can conceal convenience when people differ in bargaining power.

Later accounts make Fen of the Rotating Tables the explanation for an entire local change. The surviving record instead places this life among dependencies: an introduction supplied by another household, materials purchased on credit, and testimony given by people with reasons of their own. A biography that removes those dependencies becomes a useful legend and a poor guide to what happened. Descendants inherit evidence and expectations, rather than the ability to repeat an ancestor’s achievement. The practical question is which part of the achievement can be maintained by ordinary people after the celebrated individual is gone.

This belongs to The Houses of Unequal Stars. In 914, island reformers built a community where work rotated according to declared inclination rather than inherited household status. An observer arranged stars by color and apparent brightness, discovering that similar lights could stand at very different distances. Enthusiasts assigned household tasks according to the star table, converting a warning against superficial resemblance into a system of fixed personal destiny. Mainland patrons supplied scribes and introduced a prestigious administrative language distinct from everyday speech. A peace conference divided the islands temporarily between rival custodians. The promised review never occurred, and the community’s experiments became competing traditions on opposite sides of a supposedly provisional line.

In the connected record, [The Star Court Orchard](b007-the-star-court-orchard.md) preserves another part of this history. The terms recorded under [The Seasonal Partition Term](b007-the-seasonal-partition-term.md) delimit the local obligation; they do not grant a ruler unlimited command over the dead. The unresolved issue in 1248 is concrete: whether a common work calendar can cross the old partition without restoring either the star castes or the patrons’ exclusive scribal authority.

entries.title: The Star Court Orchard
entries.body:
Night observers used orchard walls to block lamp glare. Later priests grafted trees according to alleged stellar temperaments, ruining several varieties. Gardeners restored compatible rootstocks while keeping the observation benches, preserving useful inquiry without its failed agricultural doctrine.

The site has changed use more than once. Its surviving structures should not be read as a single intact design: one household repairs what another abandoned, and a later occupant can preserve a wall while giving its opening a different purpose. Visitors who search only for the original foundation overlook the people paying for the present roof. Custody depends on continuing access and maintenance, not merely on a persuasive genealogy. Removing an interesting object may erase evidence of a repair that explains why the place remains habitable at all.

entries.title: The Houses of Inclination
entries.body:
Households advertised chosen work and exchanged labor through a public table. Rich members could choose pleasant tasks more readily. A disputed account records who cleaned after festivals, showing the hidden work beneath declarations that everyone followed a beloved calling.

The institution’s public account emphasizes its founding purpose, while daily accounts reveal exceptions, unpaid work, and compromises with neighbors. Membership does not imply agreement. A clerk, a patron, and a laborer can defend the same arrangement for incompatible reasons. Its authority is strongest where it provides something people actually need and weakest where it claims that need as proof of permanent jurisdiction. Reform requires deciding who will perform the useful work afterward. Simply abolishing the name may leave the obligation in the hands of less accountable successors.

entries.title: The Provisional Island Division
entries.body:
Negotiators divided landing custody for one fishing season and promised a review after storm damage was assessed. The review funds financed a memorial instead. Descendants treat the division as ancient, although the founding document repeatedly describes its term as temporary.

The event survives through records made for different purposes. A household remembers hunger; a court records jurisdiction; a custodian records the interruption of an observance. Their dates can be reconciled without making their explanations identical. Later commemorations often select a decisive moment because a ceremony needs a beginning and an end. The consequences were less orderly, traveling through marriages, prices, and people who moved away. An honest account follows those consequences far enough to distinguish a temporary outcome from an agreement that still constrains the present.

entries.title: The Two Brightness Boards
entries.body:
One board lists apparent brightness; the other compares recurring changes over years. Patrons displayed only the first, making distant lights seem equivalent to near ones. The second survives in a net loft whose owner wants recognition for keeping it dry.

Material inspection places limits on the object’s legend. Repairs, wear, and changes in custody can establish that it was used repeatedly without proving every story attached to it. Its value is relational: somebody can authenticate it, somebody needs it for an observance, and somebody may suffer if it is removed. An expensive replacement would not automatically inherit those relations. Custodians therefore record loans and repairs as carefully as ceremonial appearances. A collector who purchases the object but ignores its attached undertaking may own something that cannot safely be taken home.

entries.title: The Unchosen Task Meal
entries.body:
Participants serve a meal made through tasks they would not personally choose, acknowledging dependence beyond inclination. Affluent members hire replacements. Organizers now require disclosure of paid assistance rather than claiming that private labor can be made equal by ceremony.

The custom is learned through participation rather than a single authoritative text. Households disagree about details while recognizing enough shared actions to cooperate. That flexibility can admit newcomers or allow influential families to redefine the practice in their own favor. Describing it as ancient settles neither possibility. Its practical test is whether a participant can question a demand without losing access to food, water, or witnesses. Local reformers seek finite observances whose costs can be recorded, so that reverence for predecessors does not become an unanswerable demand upon children.

entries.title: The Color Without Rank
entries.body:
An observer’s manuscript states that a star’s color supplies no household rank. Later margin notes turn the classification into a destiny chart. Readers reproduce the layers separately, allowing believers to see which authority their preferred system actually invokes.

Copies disagree in ways that matter. A shortened phrase can remove a condition, and a copied date can imply that a later amendment belonged to the original undertaking. Dry writing preserves evidence but cannot make an oath binding by itself. Readers must distinguish a record of consent from a writer’s assertion that consent occurred. Marginal notes are sometimes the only surviving testimony of people excluded from the formal version. Establishing a trustworthy reading therefore depends on comparing custody, material, and ordinary expenses, as well as elegant arguments about wording.

entries.title: The Lantern Reef Ray
entries.body:
A translucent ray follows small fish attracted by quay lamps. Star-house interpreters describe its visits as celestial confirmation. Fishers reduce lamps near its breeding shallows, demonstrating that controlling the apparent sign protects the animal without settling anybody’s cosmic beliefs.

Reports describe a living creature before they describe a supernatural emblem. It needs food, shelter, and a place to breed, and it reacts to disturbances that witnesses may misunderstand. A keeper who recognizes those needs can often prevent the encounter later remembered as a curse. The animal cannot be made into an obedient instrument of ancestral power. Where an undertaking changes its habitat, the effect is indirect and costly to other inhabitants. Stories that treat its behavior as a moral verdict obscure both ordinary suffering and the human decisions that altered the site.

entries.title: The Review Ferry
entries.body:
The ferry once transported delegates to the promised boundary review. Its seasonal landing rights remain valid despite the abandoned conference. Current passengers invoke those finite rights to cross between islands whose patrols now claim no lawful connection ever existed.

A route is an agreement between people maintaining its difficult portions, as much as a line across terrain. Tolls buy repairs only when their recipients are accountable for the work. A passage described as open may still be unusable for children, loaded animals, or travelers without an accepted witness. Seasonal detours preserve movement while distributing its costs to other households. Pilots and guides keep alternative accounts of distance because time, provisions, and exposure matter more than ceremonial measures. Closing one stretch can therefore revise obligations far beyond its immediate neighborhood.

entries.title: The Seasonal Partition Term
entries.body:
This clause expires custodial division after one season unless all named landing households renew it. Officials cite later decrees instead of renewal evidence. The law’s recovery threatens patrol income more directly than either island’s identity.

The rule’s force depends on a stated scope. It governs named acts and claimants, rather than every future disagreement that resembles its original case. Courts have nevertheless tried to extend it, usually when a narrow precedent would benefit a powerful applicant. Opponents do not have to deny ancestor law to challenge that extension. They can ask which promise was actually made, who witnessed it, and whether the required observance remains possible. The difference between a valid undertaking and a convenient assertion of authority is central to the current dispute.

entries.title: The Orchard Temperament Failure
entries.body:
Star-based grafting killed trees unevenly because rootstocks differed. Leaders blamed gardeners’ impure inclination. A surviving planting map correlates losses with graft compatibility, exposing how a flattering cosmic explanation concealed a testable practical mistake.

The event survives through records made for different purposes. A household remembers hunger; a court records jurisdiction; a custodian records the interruption of an observance. Their dates can be reconciled without making their explanations identical. Later commemorations often select a decisive moment because a ceremony needs a beginning and an end. The consequences were less orderly, traveling through marriages, prices, and people who moved away. An honest account follows those consequences far enough to distinguish a temporary outcome from an agreement that still constrains the present.

entries.title: The Rotation Tokens
entries.body:
Tokens assign unpleasant communal tasks and record substitutes. One series lacks substitute marks, making affluent households appear exemplary. Restoring the omitted marks changes who owes labor without requiring a claim that every founder acted dishonestly.

Material inspection places limits on the object’s legend. Repairs, wear, and changes in custody can establish that it was used repeatedly without proving every story attached to it. Its value is relational: somebody can authenticate it, somebody needs it for an observance, and somebody may suffer if it is removed. An expensive replacement would not automatically inherit those relations. Custodians therefore record loans and repairs as carefully as ceremonial appearances. A collector who purchases the object but ignores its attached undertaking may own something that cannot safely be taken home.

entries.title: The Two Language Supper
entries.body:
Hosts recite each undertaking in the patron’s language and a household’s chosen tongue. Mistakes are corrected before food is served. Younger speakers propose a third version for migrants, extending a custom whose original defenders once treated two languages as sufficient forever.

The custom is learned through participation rather than a single authoritative text. Households disagree about details while recognizing enough shared actions to cooperate. That flexibility can admit newcomers or allow influential families to redefine the practice in their own favor. Describing it as ancient settles neither possibility. Its practical test is whether a participant can question a demand without losing access to food, water, or witnesses. Local reformers seek finite observances whose costs can be recorded, so that reverence for predecessors does not become an unanswerable demand upon children.

entries.title: The Conference Afterword
entries.body:
A clerk preserved delegates’ disagreements beneath the formal boundary agreement. The afterword reveals doubts about maintenance funding rather than a secret wish for permanent division. Its recovery makes the missing review a failure of execution as well as political will.

Copies disagree in ways that matter. A shortened phrase can remove a condition, and a copied date can imply that a later amendment belonged to the original undertaking. Dry writing preserves evidence but cannot make an oath binding by itself. Readers must distinguish a record of consent from a writer’s assertion that consent occurred. Marginal notes are sometimes the only surviving testimony of people excluded from the formal version. Establishing a trustworthy reading therefore depends on comparing custody, material, and ordinary expenses, as well as elegant arguments about wording.

entries.title: The Stars in the Cistern
entries.body:
One courtyard cistern reflects stars displaced by irregular stonework around its lip. Islanders call the pattern a second sky. Observers use it to demonstrate how a meaningful image can arise from local geometry and still carry a household’s cherished history.

Witnesses distinguish an observed effect from their explanation for it. Repetition under comparable conditions is valuable evidence; a striking story told after its alleged cause becomes famous is weaker evidence. Masons, gardeners, and boat crews often recognize patterns an interpreter overlooks. Their explanation may reduce the immediate danger without settling whether an undertaking contributed to it. The basin has no institution capable of issuing a final answer for every manifestation. Communities record the conditions under which the effect occurs, then negotiate a response whose costs they can actually sustain.

entries.title: Night Oil Sharing
entries.body:
Observers pool lamp oil but shade every light during comparisons. Their finite supply limits meetings in winter. Patrons offer endless symbolic devotion and little oil, prompting a plain subscription ledger that values practical contributions over ceremonial pledges.

The trade depends upon tools, training, reliable materials, and people who perform work its public account barely mentions. A skilled craftsperson can improve a process, yet every batch still requires hands and a season of available materials. Output remains bounded by fuel, animals, weather, and the hands available to repair equipment. Prices carry the history of these constraints into households far from the workshop. A commercial undertaking that survives its maker can preserve useful cooperation or prevent successors from adapting to changed conditions. The present negotiation concerns how to retain knowledge while releasing an obligation nobody can now perform.

entries.title: The Border’s Missing Review
entries.body:
Landing workers demand the original review because their work calendars cross the partition. Rival custodians accuse them of abolishing tradition. The workers seek inspection of actual costs first, leaving political arrangements negotiable rather than prejudged by either accusation.

The dispute contains more than two positions. People with the same formal entitlement may face different practical costs, while opponents can depend upon the same canal, kitchen, or crossing. A complete settlement must describe an executable change rather than award a satisfying phrase to one side. Evidence about a past wrong remains necessary even when compensation cannot restore the original arrangement. Local negotiators separate immediate maintenance from the final assessment of responsibility. This allows a place to remain usable while its inhabitants continue an argument they have good reason not to abandon.
